rv.q: A breathtaking production that beautifully blends drama and comedy, it is a searing tale that unveils the disconnect between how people see themselves and who they truly are.
Playwright Branden Jacobs-Jenkins' latest is a feast of the good stuff - crackling dialogue, powerhouse ensemble acting and weighty themes delivered with biting naturalism.
But above all, of course, the show works because of Jacobs-Jenkins's writing, which is probing without losing its humor and bracingly honest without being cruel.

Purpose has arrived as Americans contemplate the dissolution of all things that once seemed permanent. Timely though it may be, it also seems destined to take its place among the greatest American dramas of all time.

Jacobs-Jenkins' brilliant blending of comedy and drama is a fascinatingly layered look at a multi-generational family with a public-facing respectability that conceals the schisms behind their carefully constructed public façade.

It's a fascinating treatise on respectability, conservatism, preservation and legacy which, in Jacobs-Jenkins fashion, is also an enthralling drama which draws the most biting comedic blood from its human tragedy.

Purpose buzzes with rich ideas about sons and fathers and the burdens of legacy, sexuality, and authenticity. Solomon Sr.'s passion for beekeeping cleverly drives home the point of the play's title. Purpose dazzles and stings.
For those of us too young to have seen Laurette Taylor in 'The Glass Menagerie,' there is now the opportunity to see LaTanya Richardson Jackson in 'Purpose.'

(Warning: The following review contains spoilers) Huntington Theatre Company kicks off its 2026-2027 season with the extraordinary play "PURPOSE," centered on a family with members trying to either escape or embrace that which defines them.
Josiah Davis has crafted an undeniable triumph of contemporary American theatre, directing Purpose with a razor-sharp sensitivity that honors the script's every nuance.
Josiah Davis directs the Huntington production, orchestrating a fine cast of six actors who richly embody their roles, as well as staging that is as eloquent as the play.
Director Josiah Davis meets the challenge of Purpose and its ambitious melding of theatrical technique and complex storyline, drawing us in and leaving us moved and inspired.
In a production at The Huntington directed by Josiah Davis, 'Purpose' registers as too much of a good thing. It's overstuffed and, at nearly three hours including an intermission, overlong.
There's a lot to like about this play, but in the end it's exhausting, and the ending featuring Naz and his father feels false.

cn.t: Critics hail Jacobs-Jenkins' Pulitzer and Tony-winning family drama as a future American classic, praising its crackling dialogue, biting humor, and searing exploration of legacy, sexuality, and authenticity within a fractured family.
